extracted.intended_audience: members of the public (potential complainants) considering lodging a complaint with the Australian Press Council
extracted.subtask_short: filing complaints to australian press council
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public on when, how and about what they may complain to the Australian Press Council, including jurisdictional limits, time limits, procedural expectations and confidentiality. Covers types of material and publishers within Council jurisdiction and practical steps for submitting complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of material that can be complained about
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints may relate to news reports, articles, editorials, letters, cartoons, images and other published material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council does not consider complaints about advertising material, except where the complaint is that the material is not clearly identifiable as advertising. Complaints about broadcasts on radio or television may be more appropriately dealt with by other organisations; the Council will suggest referral where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of publications within Council jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council considers complaints about material published in print or digital form by publishers which are 'constituent bodies' of the Council, including most Australian newspapers and magazines, associated digital outlets and some leading digital-only publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A list of constituent bodies is provided (link). Complaints about material from publishers that are not constituent bodies may be considered, but such publishers are not under a legal obligation to cooperate with the Council or to publish any adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: Global Digital Publishers exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council will not consider complaints about articles published by a Global Digital Publisher if the article does not relate to events within Australia, or does not concern an Australian national, or resident at the time of publication, who is 'directly and personally affected' by an alleged breach of the Council’s standards of practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an article has insufficient connection to Australia or directly affected Australians, the Council declines jurisdiction over that material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaints relate to publications (not individual journalists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints are treated by the Council as being against the publication, not any individual journalist or editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most complaints the Council’s consideration is likely to focus on the actions of journalists, editors or other media practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may complain (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, any person may lodge a complaint about published material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless there are exceptional circumstances, the Council will not consider complaints by one publisher member of the Council against another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary complaints (when complainant is not identified)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a complainant is not personally identified or likely to be identified by the published material, the complaint will be considered as a 'secondary complaint'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary complaints are subject to some different procedures (see Handling of Complaints).

rubrics_metrics.name: When a complaint can be made — relationship to complaining to the publication
rubrics_metrics.description: A person can complain to the Council after complaining to the relevant publication; at the same time as a complaint is made to the publication; or without having complained to the publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a complaint is made directly to the Council, it may commence consideration or in some circumstances ask the complainant to raise the complaint directly with the publication and then return to the Council if further involvement is sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media posts associated with a publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the nature of social media commentary, the Council considers that a publication should be provided with a reasonable opportunity to resolve concerns with a social media post directly with its readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complaints concerning social media posts can often be resolved quickly once the publication becomes aware of a reader's concerns; in some circumstances the Council may consider a complaint further if a complainant has not been able to resolve it directly with the publisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits for lodging complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints normally should be made within thirty days of the first publication of the relevant material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complaint can be made with a request that the Council delays consideration until a specified event (e.g. recovery from serious illness). If a complaint is lodged out of time the complainant must seek approval for consideration on the basis of one or more justifications: reasonable justification for not having noticed the material earlier; the complaint involves multiple articles over a lengthy period; the complainant had spent time unsuccessfully seeking a response from the publication; or there were other good grounds for delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of legal proceedings on Council consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council does not require complainants to undertake that they will not commence legal proceedings in relation to the material about which they are complaining, but they must tell the Council if they have done so or may do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proceedings have actually been commenced, consideration of the complaint by the Council should not proceed unless there are special circumstances which mean that a delay would be unfairly detrimental to the complainant.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to make a complaint (form and channels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints should be made by completing the Council’s Complaint Form and sending it to the Council preferably online, or by email, fax or post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact details are on the form. If it is difficult or impossible for a complainant to make a written complaint using the online or downloadable form, they may contact the Council for advice and assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and use of lawyers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council’s complaints process is intended to be as informal, prompt and economical as possible. Complaints must be made and pursued by complainants or their immediate family unless there are exceptional circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants and publications are not normally permitted to communicate with the Council through lawyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality choices for complainants
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainants must indicate when making a complaint if they wish some details to be kept confidential from the publication or not to be published in any Council adjudication on the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Council will then explain circumstances in which confidentiality may be possible and the complainant can decide whether to proceed with the complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Council will refer matters more appropriately dealt with elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it is more appropriate for a complaint to be dealt with by another organisation, the Council will suggest that the complainant raises the matter with that organisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may occur where the complaint relates to advertising, or to broadcasts on radio or television.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaints about methods of information gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council can consider complaints about the methods used by publications to obtain information which is subsequently published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such complaints fall within the Council’s remit even when the objection is to the information-gathering process rather than the content alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing unreasonable complaints and complainants (behavioural expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APC expects all complainants to treat APC staff with courtesy and respect and will not tolerate communications and conduct that put its staff and members at risk of physical or mental harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APC has a legislative responsibility to provide a safe working environment; its Policy for Managing Unreasonable Complaints and Complainants sets out how such cases are handled (link).
